transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronan.
The Justice Department has dropped an unprecedented lawsuit in California that sought to set aside
thousands of ballots.
NPR's Jude Jaffee Black reports the news comes after a series of legal losses for the federal
government in the case.
The Justice Department had wanted election officials to set aside the ballots of thousands
of people federal officials said were likely non-citizens but had not offered evidence.
Federal courts up to the U.S. Supreme Court rejected the Justice Department's request
before election day.
The parties were expected back in court next week, but the Justice Department wrote late
Friday it's voluntarily dropping the case, and noted by the time of the court hearing
the ballots in question would already be co-mingled with other ballots.
An analysis by UCLA data experts found the federal government's list of suspected non-citizens
has extensive errors and included names of people who are not registered to vote and
others who are eligible voters.
Jude Jaffee Black, NPR News.
Two U.S. Senate races are still too close to call, NPR's Ashley Lopez reports election
officials in Mississippi and Alaska continue to count ballots three days after the midterms.
Both Alaska and Mississippi have closely watched Senate races that are coming down to very
slim margins.
As of Friday at last check, Alaska's Senate race between Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan
and Democrat Mary Peltola was down to a margin of several hundred votes.
And because the races are so close, every ballot counts at this point.
Both states accept postmark late arriving mail ballots, so not all ballots are even at
election offices.
Because of the margins, many of those ballots will need to be counted before a race call
is likely and Mississippi election officials are also working through quite a few provisional
ballots.
Those are typically given to voters who face questions about their eligibility at the polls.
Ashley Lopez, NPR News.
Pope Leo is in Uruguay, the first stop on his three-country, 12-day visit to Latin
America.
NPR's Carrie Khan has more.
The crowds have been small but enthusiastic for Leo, the first papal visit in nearly four
decades to Latin America's most secular nation.
Leo didn't wait long to urge more religiosity in public life and criticized Uruguay's pioneering
law legalizing abortion.
"Whoever has not yet been born already belongs to the human family and to the future," he
said, deserving all dignity and protection.
Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholic.
Leo addressed Uruguay's public secularism with the president at his side.
He urged that religion not be confined just to the private sphere.
Carrie Khan, NPR News, Montevideo.
President Trump is replacing White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller.
Miller is the deputy chief of staff and architect of many of the president's most controversial
policies.
This is NPR.
Even as a federal judge has halted for 14 days, President Trump's proposed memorial
march between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, the White House launched
a new website Friday to promote the project.
The judge's order came after officials from Virginia and Washington, D.C., along with
a group of Vietnam veterans, sued to stop the project, arguing it is flagrantly unlawful
without the approval from Congress.
Scientists have found the earliest evidence of the people using cannabis to get high 3,000
years ago.
Here's NPR's Ned Rott.
Scythians were a nomadic people that roamed the Eurasian steppes.
And almost a decade ago, archaeologists found a massive burial mound that they made in current
day Siberia.
In it, the scientists found intact cannabis seeds and human hair from a person who lived
2,800 years ago.
They ran a drug test on the hair, because why not?
And in a new paper published in the journal Science, the archaeologists say it tested
positive for THC, the psychoactive compound in cannabis.
Researchers warn that doesn't mean the people were intentionally smoking it for the buzz,
but if so, it suggests humans have been using the plant far longer than previously believed.
Ned Rott, NPR News.
After rainfall Thursday along the Tennessee, Georgia state line caused heavy flooding on
the Toccoa River, and officials with the National Weather Service are calling this a catastrophic
once-in-a-1,000-year weather event, I'm Dan Roman, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: Justice Department drops lawsuit seeking to set aside thousands of California ballots
Alaska and Mississippi Senate races remain too close to call as ballots are counted
Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay, urging religion's role in public life and criticizing abortion law
Trump replaces White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller
Federal judge halts Trump's proposed memorial march between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington for 14 days
Scientists find 3,000-year-old evidence of cannabis use in Siberian burial mound hair
Heavy flooding on Toccoa River along Tennessee-Georgia line called once-in-1,000-year event
